name: Amber / Oriental fragrances

lead: Amber, or Oriental, is one of the main families on the Fragrance Wheel, covering sweet, warm, slightly animalic scents built on ambergris or labdanum resin and often blended with vanilla, tonka bean, flowers and woods.
People wear them as part of grooming and style, since scent contributes to the impression someone makes. Examples cited include Guerlain's Shalimar and Yves Saint Laurent's Opium.

paras: Worn as colognes, eau de parfum or oils, usually for evenings and cooler weather because the heavy notes carry far. Applied to pulse points or clothing in small amounts.

Fragrance ingredients can cause skin irritation or allergy in sensitive people. Natural ambergris is banned to trade in the US and several other countries, so modern amber scents generally use synthetic ambroxide.

angle.text: People wear amber and oriental fragrances as a finishing touch to grooming. The effect is on how a person is perceived by smell rather than sight.

lead: Amber, historically called Oriental, is a fragrance family of sweet, slightly animalic scents built on ambergris or labdanum, often combined with vanilla, tonka bean, flowers and woods [1]. Traditional examples include Guerlain's Shalimar, Yves Saint Laurent's Opium and Chanel's Coco Mademoiselle [1].

In style and grooming, fragrance is an addition to appearance: people choose a scent to project warmth, richness or sensuality, with amber notes favoured for evenings and cooler weather. The family sits on the Fragrance Wheel, created by consultant Michael Edwards in 1983, which divides perfumes into Floral, Amber, Woody, Aromatic Fougere and Fresh [1].

Natural ambergris has long been prized as a fixative; ambrein itself is nearly odourless, and its oxidation products ambroxide and ambrinol give the scent. Ambroxide is now made synthetically and widely used [2].
infobox: Vanilla, tonka bean, labdanum, ambergris, spices, resins [1]

paras: Amber-family scents are sweet and warm, sometimes with camphorous oils and incense resins [1]. Chypre perfumes straddle the Amber and Woody families on the wheel [1].

Perfumers prized ambergris as a fixative that makes scents last longer, but it has largely been replaced by synthetics [2]. Commercial trade and possession are banned in Australia, the United States and India, while it is legal in the UK, EU and Switzerland [2].

timeline.event: Michael Edwards creates the Fragrance Wheel, placing Amber as one of five families [1]
